_comment_family: ITC Avant Garde Gothic ships as a family of weights - Book, Medium,
Demi, Bold, and the obliques - and the file in fonts/ is the Medium
of it. Only that one cut is here, but the naming still has to be
done deliberately, because this file carries THREE names any of
which somebody might reach for and only two of which name this cut.
Name ID 16, the typographic family, is 'ITC Avant Garde Gothic Std',
and every weight of the family carries it. Declaring that would be
declaring a name a Book or a Bold could answer to just as well, and
on a geometric sans the weights are not a variation on the design -
the Book is a hairline-ish text weight and the Bold is a display
weight, so a caption measured against the Medium and drawn in either
would come out at a width nothing measured.
Name ID 1 is 'ITC Avant Garde Std Md', which is Adobe's abbreviated
family-plus-cut, and it names this file and no other - the 'Md' is
in it. So that is what gets declared, which is the same call
garet-book makes and for the same reason: what the file says about
itself, where what it says already names the cut.
Weight 500, which is the file's own usWeightClass and what Medium
means. Asking for 400 here would invite a browser to synthesise a
weight this family has a real drawn cut of and this folder does not
carry; asking for 700 would invite it to embolden.
_comment_css: Not declared in styles.css: this face arrived with a channel and is

_comment_local: What the machine may already know the face by, tried after the file.
The first is the PostScript name and is also what the installer
registers the face under (see engine.install_fonts, which takes the
first entry); the second is name ID 1. Both name this one cut rather
than the family, so a machine answering to either is answering with
this file - which is exactly what the fallback route is for.
Only two entries and not the usual three, because this file's full
name (ID 4) is 'ITCAvantGardeStd-Md' - the PostScript name over

reason above: it is the typographic family, and every weight of it

_comment_metrics: Three measurements, all of them for the pack that is set in this
face (content/channels/feeddrama) and none of them read by anything
at run time. They are here because the next face dropped into a
Snapchat channel will want the same ones taken, which is the habit
korolev-bold started and garamond-premier-pro-bold-italic-subhead
carried on.
The cap height is the file's own sCapHeight: 740 units of a
1000-unit em, so at the Snapchat preset's stated 40px the capitals
stand 29.6px tall. That is the number worth knowing about this face.
Garamond Premier's are 660 and Trade Gothic's are lower still, so a
caption set at 40px here reads noticeably LARGER than the same
sentence on a sibling channel at the same stated size - the nominal
size is the same and the ink is not. It was not corrected with a
size of this pack's own: the 40px is the heading's one answer to
burned-in speech (see the preset), and a face with large capitals
filling more of the line is the face being itself rather than a
number being wrong. The x-height is 554, which is the same story and
is what makes the lower case look set large even though it is never
drawn under the preset's `uppercase`.
The widths were taken on a canvas at the size the pack is set at,
which is the measurement that matters rather than a sum of advance
widths: the renderer measures the same way, so the numbers below have
whatever the browser applies in them. Worth one line on what that is
here, because this file has no kern table at all and its pairing
lives in GPOS: the two figures come out within half a pixel of each
other over twenty characters, so on this face the kerning is not what
decides anything - the face is simply wide.
Twenty mixed capitals (A to T) measure 500px against the 486px a
Snapchat line has, so like garamond-premier-pro-bold-italic-subhead
this face lands the frame's width and the preset's twenty-character
ceiling in the same place instead of the characters binding first.
Ordinary prose fits, but not with much room: twenty characters of
real sentence measure between 426px and 490px depending on what
letters are in them, because the spaces and the narrow letters an
alphabet run has none of do most of the work, and a wide sentence of
round capitals uses nearly the whole line. In practice an unusually
wide line breaks at nineteen instead of twenty, which the wrapper
does on its own and nobody sees (see the two ceilings in
js/caption.js).
The glyph check the Snapchat packs take: 433 codepoints, the
accented Latin capitals and lower case among them, so a caption
with a name in it is drawn from this file rather than from whatever
the browser substitutes for a missing glyph - which would be a
different face at a width nothing measured.
_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice - a
title laid out against the wrong metrics is broken, not merely
different, which is what fontguard exists to catch before it is ever
drawn. They are still chosen rather than copied, and here there is a
genuinely close one to choose: Century Gothic was drawn as Monotype's
answer to this exact face, single-storey a and all, and it is on
every Windows that has ever had Office on it. It is the same
fallback garet-book reaches for and for the same reason - both are
geometric sans faces built on circles.
Segoe UI stands behind it for the machine that somehow lacks even
that, and Arial behind that. Impact and Arial Black are absent for
telegraf-ultralight's reason: they are heavy condensed display cuts,
and putting one behind a 500-weight geometric would make the one
thing that survives a missing file the furthest possible thing from
